title: Living there
hookLine: "abodes": a place to live all day, not only on the cushion

cards: Visiting a place isn't the same as living there. A weekend at a friend's cabin can feel wonderful. But you don't know the cabin until a rainy Tuesday, doing the dishes, in a bad mood.
It's easy to treat kindness like that cabin: somewhere to visit during a quiet sit, before driving back to real life. The name the Buddha gave these four qualities says something else.

teach.b: Twelve days ago, brahmavihara came apart into brahma, the sublime, and vihara, a dwelling, the same word used for a monastery, where monks actually live. Take that second half at its word. The name isn't four exercises.
It's four homes. The Metta Sutta, a short discourse on kindness that Theravada monks and lay people chant, says it directly.

After describing a mind of kindness toward all beings, it says to keep this mindfulness standing, walking, sitting or lying down, for as long as you're awake, and it calls that a sublime abiding, here and now.
Standing, walking, sitting, lying down: that's the whole day. The bus stop, the grocery aisle, the moment before sleep.

teach.h: THE CUSHION TEACHES THE WAY HOME.
teach.b: The cushion is where you learn the way home; it isn't the only place home exists.
And a house you live in gets small repairs all the time. You notice the drip and fix it. Nobody lives in kindness perfectly.

You notice you've wandered into irritation, and you come back, again and again, the way you come back to your own front door at the end of the day. In this picture, the aim isn't a special feeling during meditation.
It's that, little by little, these four become the ordinary weather of a life.

how: The Metta Sutta is chanted in Theravada monasteries and homes, and teachers encourage bringing kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity into ordinary activity, walking, working and talking, not only into formal sitting.

o: holding one calm feeling without ever slipping
keeping these qualities all day, not just while sitting
moving into a monastery to practice full-time

games.q: match the pieces of the name.
p: where you learn the way home

s: the brahmaviharas are meant only for formal meditation
the Metta Sutta says to keep them standing, walking, sitting or lying down, while awake.
vihara is the same word used for a monastery
it means a dwelling, the place where you live.
everyone wanders; the practice is noticing and coming back, like small repairs in a house.

games.q: you felt deeply kind on the cushion this morning. an hour later you're snapping at a slow driver. what does the Metta Sutta's teaching suggest?
o: notice where you are, and come back home, right there in the car.
save kindness for the next sit.
games.why: the sutta asks for kindness standing, walking, sitting, lying down: the car is part of the house.

practice: Picture your day ahead with four checkpoints, morning, midday, afternoon and evening, each one a single breath and one question: where am I living right now, in kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, or somewhere else?
Try the first one now: one breath, no judging the answer. Just notice it, and turn toward home.

wordCard.voice: Living there. Vihara means a dwelling: the four immeasurables are homes to live in all day, not places to visit.

orig.note: Pali brahmavihāra: a sublime dwelling, a place to live, not just visit.

carryVoice: Your line: live there. The four are homes, not weekend cabins. That's two hundred forty-four days.
